items.title: The Governor — office, powers and assent to bills
items.body:
### The Governor

**In one line**
The Governor is the constitutional (nominal) head of a state — the state-level counterpart of the President — while the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers hold the real power.

**Why it is asked**
Appointment, the term "during the President's pleasure", who the Governor appoints, the Art 200 assent options and the Art 161 pardon limits are heavily tested.

**The story**
Article 153 makes the Governor the head of each state. The President appoints the Governor (Art 155) for a five-year term, but the Governor actually holds office **during the President's pleasure** (Art 156) — there is no fixed removal procedure, so a Governor can be moved at any time. A Governor must be a citizen of India, at least **35 years** old, and not a member of any legislature or a holder of an office of profit.

All executive action of the state runs in the Governor's name (Art 154). The Governor appoints the Chief Minister and, on the CM's advice, the other ministers, and also appoints the Advocate General (Art 165), the State Election Commissioner and the members of the State Public Service Commission, and is Chancellor of the state universities. In the legislature the Governor summons, prorogues and dissolves the Houses, addresses them, and nominates expert members to the Council. The pardon power (Art 161) covers offences under **state** law only — the Governor **cannot pardon a death sentence** and has **no** power over court-martial cases.

**Picture it**

| Option under Art 200 | Effect |
|---|---|
| Assent | Bill becomes law |
| Withhold assent | Bill ends |
| Return (not a money bill) | Legislature reconsiders; if re-passed, Governor must assent |
| Reserve for the President | Art 201 then applies |

**Terms explained**
- **Nominal (constitutional) head** = the formal head who normally acts on ministers' advice, not the real decision-maker.
- **During the President's pleasure** = the Governor can be removed at any time by the Centre; there is no fixed tenure guarantee.
- **Office of profit** = a paid post under the government that would disqualify the holder.

**Don't confuse**
- The Governor's pardon (Art 161) is **narrower** than the President's (Art 72): no death-sentence pardon and no court-martial power.
- **Judges of the High Court** are appointed by the **President**, not the Governor — a common trap.

**Remember it**
"Centre's appointee, neutral umpire" — chosen and removable by the Centre, yet meant to act as a neutral constitutional head. The 2023 Punjab Governor case said a Governor withholding assent must return the bill with reasons and cannot sit on it indefinitely.

**TL;DR**
- Governor = constitutional head of the state (Art 153); appointed by the President (Art 155), holds office during the President's pleasure (Art 156); minimum age 35.
- Executive action runs in the Governor's name (Art 154); appoints the CM, ministers, Advocate General, SEC and SPSC members; Chancellor of universities.
- Art 200: assent, withhold, return (non-money bills) or reserve for the President.
- Pardon (Art 161) covers state law only — no death-sentence or court-martial pardon.
keyPoints: Governor = constitutional head of the state (Art 153); appointed by the President (Art 155) for 5 years, during President's pleasure (Art 156).
Minimum age 35; must not be a legislator or hold an office of profit.
Executive actions run in the Governor's name (Art 154); he appoints CM, ministers, Advocate General, SEC and SPSC members; is Chancellor of universities.
Art 200: Governor may assent, withhold, return (non-money bills) or reserve a bill for the President; if a returned bill is re-passed he must assent.
Pardoning power (Art 161) covers state law only; the Governor cannot pardon a death sentence and has no court-martial power.
104th Amendment (2019) ended nomination of an Anglo-Indian member to state Assemblies.

items.title: Governor's ordinance power and discretion vs the President
items.body:
### The Governor's Ordinance Power and Discretion

**In one line**
When the legislature is not sitting the Governor can make temporary laws (ordinances), and in a few defined situations the Governor acts on personal judgement rather than on ministers' advice.

**Why it is asked**
The extra "President's instructions" check on state ordinances, and the exact list of the Governor's discretionary powers, are frequent statement-based questions.

**The story**
The Governor's **ordinance power (Article 213)** mirrors the President's (Art 123) but with one extra leash. An ordinance can be issued only when the assembly (if the state is unicameral) or **both Houses** (if bicameral) are not in session. It has the same force as a law, is coextensive with the state legislature's power, and **ceases six weeks after the legislature reassembles** (or earlier if the House disapproves it). Unlike the President, the Governor must obtain the **President's instructions** before issuing certain ordinances — for example, ones that would otherwise need to be reserved for the President.

In normal matters the Governor follows the Council of Ministers, but in defined situations the Governor has real **discretion**: choosing a Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority, dismissing a CM who has clearly lost confidence, reserving a bill for the President, and recommending **President's Rule (Art 356)**. Under Art 163, if a question arises whether a matter falls within the Governor's discretion, the Governor's decision is final.

**Picture it**

| Situation | Governor acts on |
|---|---|
| Ordinary executive business | Council of Ministers' advice |
| Hung assembly — choosing a CM | Own discretion |
| Reserving a bill / recommending Art 356 | Own discretion |
| Certain ordinances | The President's instructions |

**Terms explained**
- **Ordinance** = a temporary law made by the executive when the legislature is not in session; it must later be approved by the legislature.
- **Coextensive** = the ordinance can cover exactly the same subjects the state legislature itself could legislate on.
- **President's Rule (Art 356)** = central rule imposed when a state's constitutional machinery fails.

**Don't confuse**
- The Governor's ordinance power carries a **President's-instructions** check that the President's own power (Art 123) does not.
- "During the President's pleasure" is about the Governor's tenure; "President's instructions" is about certain ordinances — different ideas.

**Remember it**
"The Governor's ordinance has a second lock" — the President's instructions. The Sarkaria (1988) and Punchhi (2010) Commissions urged non-partisan Governors and sparing use of Art 356.

**TL;DR**
- Art 213: the Governor issues ordinances only when the House(s) are not in session; they lapse six weeks after reassembly.
- Certain state ordinances need the President's instructions — a check the President does not face.
- Discretion: a CM in a hung assembly, dismissing a CM without a majority, reserving bills, recommending Art 356.
- Art 163 makes the Governor's view on his own discretion final; Sarkaria and Punchhi urged restraint.
keyPoints: Art 213: Governor promulgates ordinances only when the House(s) are not in session; they lapse 6 weeks after reassembly.
Governor's ordinance power needs the President's instructions in certain cases — a check the President does not face.
Governor's discretion: choosing a CM in a hung assembly, dismissing a CM without majority, reserving bills, recommending President's Rule (Art 356).
Art 163: the Governor's decision on what falls within his discretion is final and non-justiciable.
Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions urged non-partisan Governors and sparing use of Article 356.

items.title: Chief Minister and the State Council of Ministers
items.body:
### Chief Minister and the State Council of Ministers

**In one line**
The Chief Minister is the real head of the state government, leading a Council of Ministers that is answerable to the elected Legislative Assembly.

**Why it is asked**
Articles 163/164/177, the 91st Amendment's 15% cap with a floor of 12, and collective responsibility are standard exam points.

**The story**
The **Chief Minister** is appointed by the Governor under **Article 164**. The Constitution lays down no procedure, so by convention the Governor invites the leader of the majority party; in a hung assembly the Governor uses discretion and asks for a floor test. The CM is the real executive and the link between the Governor and the ministry.

The **Council of Ministers** works on three constitutional rules. **Art 163** says the Council, headed by the CM, aids and advises the Governor. **Art 164** says the CM is appointed by the Governor and the other ministers on the CM's advice, and that ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure. The **91st Amendment (2003)** caps the total number of ministers, including the CM, at **15% of the Assembly's strength**, with a **minimum of 12**, and bars anyone disqualified for defection from being made a minister. **Art 177** lets a minister speak in either House but vote only in the House to which he belongs. The ministry has three ranks — Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers — and only the Cabinet Ministers form the Cabinet.

**Picture it**

| Provision | Content |
|---|---|
| Art 163 | Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor |
| Art 164 | Appointment of the CM and ministers; 91st Amendment 15% cap, minimum 12 |
| Art 177 | Ministers may speak in either House, vote only in their own |

**Terms explained**
- **Collective responsibility** = the whole Council stands or falls together before the Legislative Assembly.
- **Floor test** = a vote in the Assembly to prove a government commands a majority.
- **Defection** = switching parties against the anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule).

**Don't confuse**
- Collective responsibility is to the **Legislative Assembly** only (the popular House), not the Council.
- A no-confidence motion forces **all** ministers to resign, **including** those drawn from the Legislative Council — not just the MLAs.

**Remember it**
"15 percent, floor of 12" — the ministry can be at most 15% of the Assembly but never fewer than 12.

**TL;DR**
- The CM is appointed by the Governor (Art 164); the Council aids and advises the Governor (Art 163).
- 91st Amendment (2003): ministers ≤ 15% of Assembly strength, minimum 12; defectors barred.
- Art 177: ministers speak in either House, vote only in their own; three ranks, Cabinet is the inner core.
- Collective responsibility to the Legislative Assembly; a no-confidence motion makes every minister resign.
keyPoints: CM appointed by the Governor under Art 164; real executive authority and head of government.
Art 163 = Council aids and advises the Governor; advice is not enquirable in court.
91st Amendment 2003: ministers (incl. CM) ≤ 15% of Assembly strength, minimum 12; defectors barred from ministership.
Three ranks — Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, Deputy Ministers; only Cabinet Ministers form the Cabinet.
Collective responsibility is to the Legislative Assembly; a no-confidence motion makes all ministers resign.
A non-member can be made a minister but must become a legislator within six months.

items.title: State Legislature — structure, Assembly and Council
items.body:
### State Legislature — Structure, Assembly and Council

**In one line**
Every state has a legislature (Part VI); some are unicameral (Assembly only) and a few are bicameral (Assembly plus a Legislative Council).

**Why it is asked**
Article 170 (Assembly 500/60), Article 171 (Council composition and the one-third rule) and Article 169 (creating or abolishing a Council) are repeat favourites.

**The story**
The state legislature is governed by **Part VI, Articles 168-212**. **Article 169** lets Parliament create or abolish a Legislative Council if the state Assembly first passes a **special-majority resolution** — and such a change counts as ordinary law, not a constitutional amendment under Art 368.

The **Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha)** is directly elected. Under **Article 170** it has a maximum of **500** and a minimum of **60** members (small states such as Goa and Sikkim have fewer by special provision). Its term is **five years (Article 172)**, but the Governor can dissolve it earlier, and during a national emergency the term can be extended one year at a time.

The **Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)** is a **permanent body**: one-third of its members retire every two years and members serve six-year terms. Under **Article 171** its strength cannot exceed **one-third of the Assembly** and cannot be below **40**. Its make-up is mostly indirect, as the table shows, so **5/6 are elected and 1/6 nominated**.

**Picture it**

| Council category | Share |
|---|---|
| Elected by MLAs | 1/3 |
| Elected by local bodies | 1/3 |
| Elected by graduates | 1/12 |
| Elected by teachers | 1/12 |
| Nominated by the Governor | 1/6 |

**Terms explained**
- **Unicameral / bicameral** = a legislature with one House / with two Houses.
- **Special-majority resolution (Art 169)** = passed by a majority of the Assembly's total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting.
- **Permanent body** = never dissolved as a whole; members retire in staggered batches.

**Don't confuse**
- A Council's maximum is **one-third of the Assembly** (not one-half), with a floor of **40**.
- Creating or abolishing a Council (Art 169) is **ordinary law**, so it is **not** an Art 368 amendment — a frequent trap.

**Remember it**
"Assembly 500/60, Council one-third/40" — the four numbers to carry into the exam. Money Bills start only in the Assembly, and there is no joint sitting at the state level.

**TL;DR**
- State legislature = Part VI (Art 168-212); unicameral or bicameral.
- Art 170: Assembly max 500, min 60, five-year term (Art 172).
- Art 171: Council <= 1/3 of Assembly (min 40), permanent, 1/3 retire every two years; 5/6 elected, 1/6 nominated.
- Art 169: Parliament creates/abolishes a Council on the Assembly's special-majority resolution (ordinary law).
keyPoints: State legislature = Part VI, Articles 168-212; can be unicameral or bicameral.
Art 169: Parliament creates/abolishes a Council on the Assembly's special-majority resolution; not an Art 368 amendment.
Assembly (Art 170): max 500, min 60 members; tenure 5 years (Art 172).
Council (Art 171): a permanent body, one-third retire every two years, six-year terms; strength ≤ 1/3 of Assembly (min 40).
Council composition: 1/3 MLAs, 1/3 local bodies, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/6 nominated — 5/6 elected, 1/6 nominated.
Money Bills originate only in the Assembly; the Council can only recommend amendments; no joint sitting at state level.

items.title: Membership — qualifications, disqualifications and defection
items.body:
### Membership — Qualifications, Disqualifications and Defection

**In one line**
This covers who can become a member of a state legislature, what gets a member disqualified, and how the anti-defection law works.

**Why it is asked**
The age floors (25/30), who decides defection, and the Lily Thomas (2013) ruling on Section 8(4) are common statement-based questions.

**The story**
To stand for the **Legislative Assembly** a person must be a citizen of India and at least **25 years** old; for the **Legislative Council** the minimum is **30 years**. The candidate must be an elector in the state, with other qualifications set by Parliament.

A member is **disqualified** for holding an office of profit (except as a minister or an exempted office), being of unsound mind, being an undischarged insolvent, not being a citizen, or under any law made by Parliament. Under the Representation of the People Act 1951 a person is also disqualified for conviction for certain offences (two years' imprisonment or more), failing to lodge election expenses, or having a government-contract interest.

Under the **anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule)**, a member who defects is disqualified; the decision is taken by the **Speaker** (Assembly) or **Chairman** (Council), not the Governor — and the 1992 Supreme Court ruling (Kihoto Hollohan) made that decision open to judicial review. In **Lily Thomas (2013)** the Supreme Court struck down **Section 8(4)** of the RPA, so a convicted legislator is disqualified from the **date of conviction**, ending the earlier protection during appeal.

**Picture it**

| Point | Rule |
|---|---|
| Minimum age — Assembly | 25 years |
| Minimum age — Council | 30 years |
| Defection decided by | Speaker / Chairman (not the Governor) |
| Section 8(4) RPA | Struck down (Lily Thomas, 2013) |

**Terms explained**
- **Office of profit** = a paid government post that disqualifies the holder (ministers are exempt).
- **Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule)** = rules that disqualify a member for switching parties.
- **Section 8(4), RPA 1951** = the clause (now void) that once shielded a sitting member from immediate disqualification on conviction.

**Don't confuse**
- Defection is decided by the **presiding officer**, not the Governor.
- The minimum age is **25 for the Assembly** but **30 for the Council** — do not swap them.

**Remember it**
"25 lower house, 30 upper house; a convict is out from day one" — the age floors, plus the Lily Thomas rule.

**TL;DR**
- Age: 25 (Assembly), 30 (Council); must be a citizen and an elector in the state.
- Disqualified for office of profit, unsound mind, insolvency, non-citizenship, or under parliamentary law / RPA 1951.
- Defection (Tenth Schedule) decided by the Speaker/Chairman, subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992).
- Lily Thomas (2013) struck down Section 8(4): disqualification runs from the date of conviction.
keyPoints: Age: 25 years for the Assembly, 30 years for the Council; must be a citizen and an elector in the state.
Disqualified for office of profit, unsound mind, insolvency, non-citizenship, or under parliamentary law.
Defection disqualification (Tenth Schedule) decided by the Speaker/Chairman, not the Governor.
1992 SC ruling: the presiding officer's defection decision is subject to judicial review.
Section 8(4) RPA struck down in 2013 — disqualification runs from the date of conviction.
Seat vacated by double membership, resignation, 60-day absence, void election, expulsion, or becoming Governor/President/VP.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh angle — Assembly, Council and Governor
items.body:
### Andhra Pradesh Angle — Assembly, Council and Governor

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh is a working example of the state-legislature rules: a bicameral legislature at Amaravati whose Council has been abolished and revived — a live case study of Article 169.

**Why it is asked**
AP-specific numbers (175 and 58 seats) and the Council's abolition-and-revival story are exactly the kind of state-plus-polity facts APPSC favours.

**The story**
Andhra Pradesh has a **bicameral** legislature seated at **Amaravati**. The **Legislative Assembly** has **175 elected members** — down from 294 in the undivided state, because the 2014 bifurcation gave Telangana 119 seats. It is directly elected for a five-year term (Art 172).

The **Legislative Council (Sasana Mandali)** has **58 seats**, about one-third of the Assembly, satisfying Article 171. Its history is the clearest illustration of **Article 169**: the Council existed **1958-1985**, was **abolished in 1985** under N. T. Rama Rao's government, and was **revived in 2007** under Y. S. Rajasekhara Reddy — showing how a Council can be created or abolished through an Assembly resolution plus a parliamentary Act.

The **Governor** is AP's constitutional head (Art 153); the **Chief Minister**, leader of the majority party in the 175-member Assembly, heads the real executive. AP thus illustrates the Governor's Art 200 assent role, Art 213 ordinances and Art 356 recommendation power in a state setting.

**Picture it**

| House | Strength | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Legislative Assembly | 175 | Directly elected; five-year term |
| Legislative Council | 58 | About one-third of the Assembly (Art 171) |

**Terms explained**
- **Bifurcation** = the 2014 split of united Andhra Pradesh into Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
- **Sasana Mandali** = the Telugu name for the Legislative Council.
- **Article 169** = the provision for creating or abolishing a state Legislative Council.

**Don't confuse**
- 294 was the **undivided** state's Assembly; present AP has **175** and Telangana **119**.
- The 58-seat figure is the **Council**, not the Assembly.

**Remember it**
"175 and 58, abolished '85, revived '07" — AP's Assembly, Council and the Article 169 timeline.

**TL;DR**
- AP has a bicameral legislature at Amaravati: Assembly 175, Council 58.
- Undivided AP had 294 Assembly seats; after 2014, AP has 175 and Telangana 119.
- AP Council: existed 1958-1985, abolished 1985 (NTR), revived 2007 (YSR) — a textbook Article 169 case.
- The 58-seat Council is about one-third of the 175-seat Assembly (Art 171).
keyPoints: AP has a bicameral legislature at Amaravati: Assembly 175 seats, Legislative Council 58 seats.
Undivided AP Assembly had 294 seats; after the 2014 bifurcation AP has 175 and Telangana 119.
AP Legislative Council existed 1958-1985, was abolished in 1985, and was revived in 2007 — a textbook Article 169 case.
The 58-seat Council is about one-third of the 175-member Assembly, consistent with Article 171.
AP's CM is the leader of the majority party in the 175-member Assembly; the Governor is the constitutional head (Art 153).
items.source: Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly & Legislative Council — verified online (Sep 2026); Article 169

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Legislature & Executive — State Snapshot (2026)
items.body:
### Andhra Pradesh Legislature & Executive — State Snapshot (2026)

**In one line**
A current who's-who of Andhra Pradesh's executive and legislature as of 2026, with the facts most likely to appear in a dated "as-of" question.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC often asks for the sitting Governor, Chief Minister, Speaker and Council Chairman, and the AP Council's recent abolition attempt — all current-affairs-flavoured polity.

**The story**
As of 2026 the **Governor** of Andhra Pradesh is **Justice (Retd) S. Abdul Nazeer**, a former Supreme Court judge, in office since **24 February 2023**, with the Raj Bhavan at **Vijayawada**. He is the nominal head; real power lies with the **Chief Minister and Council of Ministers** (Art 163-164), appointed by the Governor under Art 164 and collectively responsible to the Assembly.

The legislature is bicameral and based in the **Amaravati** region. The **Legislative Assembly** has **175** elected members and is presided over by a Speaker; the **Legislative Council** has **58** seats (50 elected plus 8 nominated), is a permanent House under Art 171, and is presided over by a Chairman.

The Council's recent history matters: it existed 1958-1985, was abolished in 1985 and revived in 2007. A fresh **abolition resolution (2020)** passed by the Assembly was sent to the Centre, but no Act of Parliament followed, so it was **later not pursued** — the Council continues. **President's Rule (Art 356)** has been imposed in AP in **1973** (the Jai Andhra agitation) and **2014** (the impasse before bifurcation).

**Picture it**

| House | Strength | Presiding officer | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legislative Assembly | 175 elected | Speaker | Dissolvable; 5-year term (Art 172) |
| Legislative Council | 58 (50 elected + 8 nominated) | Chairman | Permanent (Art 171); 1/3 retire every 2 years |

**Terms explained**
- **Raj Bhavan** = the official residence and office of a state's Governor.
- **Abolition resolution (Art 169)** = an Assembly resolution asking Parliament to abolish the Council; it needs a further Act of Parliament to take effect.
- **President's Rule (Art 356)** = direct central rule when a state's constitutional machinery fails.

**Don't confuse**
- The **Speaker** presides over the Assembly; the **Chairman** presides over the Council — different officers.
- The 2020 abolition resolution was **never enacted**; the AP Council still exists.

**Remember it**
"Nazeer in Raj Bhavan, 175 and 58 at Amaravati" — the sitting Governor plus the two House strengths.

**TL;DR**
- AP Governor (2026): Justice (Retd) S. Abdul Nazeer, since 24 Feb 2023, Raj Bhavan Vijayawada.
- Assembly 175 (Speaker); Legislative Council 58 = 50 elected + 8 nominated (Chairman), a permanent House.
- Council abolished 1985, revived 2007; the 2020 abolition resolution was never enacted and later dropped.
- President's Rule in AP: 1973 (Jai Andhra) and 2014 (pre-bifurcation).
keyPoints: AP Governor (Sep 2026): Justice (Retd) S. Abdul Nazeer, since 24 Feb 2023, Raj Bhavan Vijayawada
AP Assembly = 175 elected seats; Speaker presides; 5-year term (Art 172)
AP Legislative Council = 58 seats (50 elected + 8 nominated); permanent house; Chairman presides
AP Council abolished 1985, revived 2007; 2020 abolition resolution never enacted and later dropped
President's Rule in AP imposed in 1973 (Jai Andhra) and 2014 (pre-bifurcation)
items.source: Official AP Govt / Constitution; incumbents verified via Wikipedia (Governor of AP, AP Legislative Council) as of Sep 2026

items.title: Chief Secretary, Governor's Immunity & Speaker on Dissolution
items.body:
### Chief Secretary, Governor's Immunity and the Speaker on Dissolution

**In one line**
Three precise facts the exam likes: who appoints the Chief Secretary, the Governor's legal immunity, and what happens to the Speaker when the Assembly is dissolved.

**Why it is asked**
Each is a clean true/false hook — appointment authority, Article 361 immunity, and the Speaker's continuity.

**The story**
The **Chief Secretary** is the administrative head of the state secretariat. He is **appointed by the Chief Minister** (not the Governor) and has **no fixed statutory tenure** — he serves at the government's discretion.

Under **Article 361**, the Governor enjoys legal **immunity** during the term of office: the Governor is **not answerable to any court** for the exercise of powers, and **no criminal proceedings** can be started or continued against the Governor while in office.

When the Legislative Assembly is **dissolved**, the **Speaker does not vacate office immediately**. He continues **until just before the first meeting of the newly elected Assembly**, which ensures there is always a presiding authority to manage the transition.

**Picture it**

| Office / event | Rule |
|---|---|
| Chief Secretary | Appointed by the CM; no fixed tenure |
| Governor (Art 361) | Immune from criminal proceedings during the term |
| Speaker on dissolution | Continues until just before the new Assembly's first meeting |

**Terms explained**
- **Chief Secretary** = the senior-most civil servant and administrative head of the state government.
- **Immunity (Art 361)** = protection from being sued or prosecuted in a court for official acts while in office.
- **Dissolution** = ending the life of the Assembly, after which fresh elections are held.

**Don't confuse**
- The Chief Secretary is appointed by the **Chief Minister**, not the Governor.
- The Speaker stays on **after** dissolution; he does **not** vacate the moment the Assembly is dissolved.

**Remember it**
"CM picks the Chief Secretary; the Speaker never leaves a gap" — continuity until the new House meets.

**TL;DR**
- The Chief Secretary is appointed by the Chief Minister and has no fixed statutory tenure.
- Art 361: the Governor is immune from criminal proceedings during the term of office.
- The Assembly Speaker continues after dissolution until just before the first meeting of the new Assembly.
keyPoints: The Chief Secretary is appointed by the Chief Minister and has no fixed statutory tenure.
Under Art 361 the Governor enjoys immunity from criminal proceedings during the term of office.
The Assembly Speaker continues in office after dissolution until just before the first meeting of the new Assembly.

items.title: For Mains — State Executive & Legislature
items.body:
### For Mains — State Executive and Legislature

**In one line**
Mains here centres on one live tension — the Governor as a source of Centre-State friction — plus the worth of a second chamber and the health of collective responsibility.

**Why it is asked (Mains clauses M3-1, M3-2 and M3-4)**
Paper-3 lists Union and State functions (M3-1), the **federal structure and the role of the Governor** (M3-2), and State Legislatures' structure, powers and privileges (M3-4). Questions are analytical and reform-oriented.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| The problem | Governor as a central appointee; delays on assent, Art 356 misuse, partisan CM invitations |
| Significance | A second chamber as a house of review; collective responsibility as accountability |
| Judgments | S. R. Bommai (1994); Nabam Rebia (2016); Punjab Governor case (2023); Shamsher Singh (1974) |
| Reforms | Sarkaria and Punchhi safeguards — timelines on assent, non-partisan selection, floor-test rules |

**Data and authorities to quote**
- Sarkaria Commission (1988): appoint eminent, non-partisan Governors; use Art 356 as a last resort.
- Punchhi Commission (2010): a fixed timeline for assent to bills, a defined floor-test procedure, and provision to impeach a Governor.
- Judgments: S. R. Bommai (1994) made Art 356 justiciable; the 2023 Punjab Governor case said a Governor must return a withheld bill with reasons; Nabam Rebia (2016) curbed the Governor's discretion on summoning the House.
- 91st Amendment (2003): the 15% cap on the state ministry.

**The AP angle**
Andhra Pradesh's Legislative Council — abolished in 1985 and revived in 2007 under Article 169 — is a ready case study on whether a second chamber adds review value or merely tracks the ruling party's convenience.

**Use in answers**
- Example: cite Tamil Nadu's and Kerala's assent disputes alongside the 2023 Punjab ruling.
- Quote: the Governor should be a "constitutional umpire, not the Centre's agent".
- Diagram idea: a bill under Art 200/201 (assent, withhold, return, reserve) and where delay creeps in.

**TL;DR**
- Centre the Governor answer on friction and the Sarkaria-Punchhi reforms.
- Quote S. R. Bommai (1994) and the 2023 Punjab Governor case.
- Use AP's Legislative Council (Art 169) as the second-chamber case study.
keyPoints: Mains clauses M3-1, M3-2 and M3-4 test the Governor-federalism tension and reform, not recall.
Dimensions to use: the problem, significance, judgments, reforms.
Quote Sarkaria (1988), Punchhi (2010), S. R. Bommai (1994) and the 2023 Punjab Governor case.
AP angle: the Legislative Council (abolished 1985, revived 2007) as a second-chamber case study.
items.source: Sarkaria Commission (1988); Punchhi Commission (2010); S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
